title: The light of the self
hookLine: a king asks what light a person has, and takes the lights away one at a time
carry: the atman is a person's own light
tomorrow: dreaming — the self creates its own world
last: THE ROOT OF A PERSON IS KNOWING AND JOY.

cards: The power goes out at night. The streetlights die, the screens go black, your phone is at one percent and then it's gone. You can't see your own hand.
Then, from the next room, someone calls your name, and you get up and walk toward the voice.
Something very like that moment is in the Brihadaranyaka, in a talk between a king and a sage with no crowd and no cows: King Janaka, asking one question and taking the lights away one by one.

teach.h: THE SUN, THE MOON, THE FIRE.
teach.b: The debate is over. In book four, Yajnavalkya visits the king again, quietly. Yajnavalkya, Janaka asks, what light does a person have?
The sun, your majesty. By the light of the sun a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. True.
But when the sun has set, what light does a person have? The moon. And when the moon has set too?
Fire. And when the fire has gone out? Speech.

teach.h: SPEECH: WE WALK TOWARD A VOICE.
teach.b: That's why, when you can't even see your own hand, wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. True, Yajnavalkya.
And when the sun and the moon have set, the fire has gone out, and speech has fallen silent, what light does a person have then? And Yajnavalkya says: atmaivasya jyotir bhavati.
The self is their light. Which is the self? The one made of knowing, the light within the heart.
That's the teaching: the atman isn't something you see; it's the seeing, the light under all the others. You can watch Hindus live it.
Many families light a diya, a small oil lamp, at the home shrine at dusk, and on Diwali they fill the house with them. Teachers often explain the outer flame as a reminder of this inner one.
And a prayer many Hindus know by heart comes from this same Upanishad: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya.

teach.h: THE ATMAN IS A PERSON'S OWN LIGHT.
teach.b: Lead me from darkness to light.

how: Hindu homes and temples light lamps at dawn and dusk and at festivals, and teachers sometimes quote the Brihadaranyaka's line that the self is a person's own light when explaining the inner meaning of the lamp.

o: a sacred flame kept burning at home
the voice you follow in the dark
light; the self is a person's own light

games.q: the lights, in order — tap the pairs.

s: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, lead me from darkness to light, comes from this same Upanishad
it's in the Brihadaranyaka's first book, 1.3.28.
Yajnavalkya calls the self the light within the heart
the one made of knowing, among the senses.
when every outer light is gone, the text says a person has no light

games.q: it's pitch dark. no sun, no moon, no fire. you can't see your own hand. how does the text say you find your way?
games.why: wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. speech is a light too, until it falls silent and only the self is left.

practice: Close your eyes and take the lights away in the king's order: let the sun set, then the moon, then let a small fire go out.
Listen for a voice, near or far, the light you'd walk toward in the dark; then let even the voices go quiet, outside and inside, and rest in whatever is left, still knowing.
If you pray, say it once, softly: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya. If not, just notice what's still lit.

wordCard.voice: Jyotis, light. The king's question and the sage's answer: when every outer light is gone, jyotis, the light a person still has, is the self.

orig.note: Sanskrit jyotis: light. ātmaivāsya jyotir bhavati, the self is their light (4.3.6).

carryVoice: Your line: the atman is a person's own light. Next, the light that shows a dream. See you tomorrow.
